Yoruba.title: Unit 1
Yoruba.subtitle: Greetings
Yoruba.tip: Yoruba greets by the time of day: Ẹ káàárọ̀ (morning), Ẹ káàsán (afternoon), Ẹ káalẹ́ (evening). "Ẹ" is the respectful form for elders; with friends drop it: "Káàárọ̀".

Yoruba.title: Unit 2
Yoruba.subtitle: Introductions
Yoruba.tip: Yoruba has three tones: high (á), mid (a) and low (à). The same letters with different tones are different words, so listen closely and copy the melody.

Yoruba.title: Unit 3
Yoruba.subtitle: Family
Yoruba.tip: Elders are never called by their first name. Children say "Màámi" (my mother) and "Bàbá mi" (my father), and greet elders kneeling (girls) or prostrating (boys).

Yoruba.title: Unit 4
Yoruba.subtitle: Numbers
Yoruba.tip: Counting for money often goes in twenties and fives in traditional Yoruba. Today most people use these numbers 1 to 10 and English numbers for big prices.

Yoruba.title: Unit 5
Yoruba.subtitle: Food and market
Yoruba.tip: Bargaining in the market is normal and friendly. Start with a smile, greet the seller first, then ask "Èló ni?".

Yoruba.title: Unit 6
Yoruba.subtitle: At home
Yoruba.tip: "Wọlé" (come in) and "Jókòó" (sit down) are what a good host says first. Visitors are usually offered water or food straight away.

Yoruba.title: Unit 7
Yoruba.subtitle: Time and weather
Yoruba.tip: Ọ̀la (tomorrow) and Àná (yesterday) are said without a word for "on": "Màá wá ní ọ̀la" means "I will come tomorrow".

Yoruba.title: Unit 8
Yoruba.subtitle: Questions and actions
Yoruba.tip: Questions often start with the question word and use "ni": "Kí ni?" (what is it), "Ta ni?" (who is it), "Ibo ni?" (where is it).

Yoruba.title: Unit 9
Yoruba.subtitle: Feelings and body
Yoruba.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Yoruba.tip: "Ó rẹ̀ mí" literally says "it tires me": in Yoruba, many feelings happen TO you, so "mí" (me) comes at the end.

Yoruba.title: Unit 10
Yoruba.subtitle: Travel and help
Yoruba.about: Find your way and ask for help
Yoruba.tip: Directions often use landmarks: a junction, a church, a big tree. Ọ̀tún is right and Òsì is left; "Lọ tààrà" means go straight.

Hausa.title: Unit 1
Hausa.subtitle: Greetings
Hausa.tip: Hausa greetings are long and warm: after "Sannu" people ask about your health, family and work. "Lafiya lau" (very well) answers almost every question.

Hausa.title: Unit 2
Hausa.subtitle: Introductions
Hausa.tip: Hausa marks who you talk to: "sunanka" is "your name" to a man, "sunanki" to a woman. The same -ka / -ki ending appears in "kake / kike" and "ka / ki".

Hausa.title: Unit 3
Hausa.subtitle: Family
Hausa.tip: Hausa letters ɓ, ɗ and ƙ are "glottal" sounds made with a little catch in the throat. They change meaning, so they matter.

Hausa.title: Unit 4
Hausa.subtitle: Numbers
Hausa.tip: Prices are often said in "naira" or the old unit "sisi". "Nawa ne?" means "how much is it?" and is the most useful market question.

Hausa.title: Unit 5
Hausa.subtitle: Food and market
Hausa.tip: Bargaining is expected. Start at about half the first price and meet in the middle with a smile and "Don Allah, ka rage".

Hausa.title: Unit 6
Hausa.subtitle: At home
Hausa.tip: Shoes come off before you enter many homes and every mosque. Greet the household before sitting.

Hausa.title: Unit 7
Hausa.subtitle: Time and weather
Hausa.tip: Times of day: safiya (morning), rana (midday), yamma (afternoon to evening), dare (night). Prayer times also mark the day.

Hausa.title: Unit 8
Hausa.subtitle: Questions and actions
Hausa.tip: Questions often end with "ne" (for a man or thing) or "ce" (for a woman): "Wane ne?" (who is he?), "Wace ce?" (who is she?).

Hausa.title: Unit 9
Hausa.subtitle: Feelings and body
Hausa.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Hausa.tip: "Na gaji" (I am tired) uses "na", the "I did / I am" marker for finished actions and states.

Hausa.title: Unit 10
Hausa.subtitle: Travel and help
Hausa.about: Find your way and ask for help
Hausa.tip: "A sauka lafiya" literally says "may you land safely" - said to anyone setting out on a journey.

Igbo.title: Unit 1
Igbo.subtitle: Greetings
Igbo.tip: "Ndewo" is a polite hello for anyone; "Nnọọ" means welcome. "Kedu?" alone is a friendly "how is it?" between friends.

Igbo.title: Unit 2
Igbo.subtitle: Introductions
Igbo.tip: Igbo is tonal: high and low tones change meaning. Akwa can be "bed", "egg", "cloth" or "crying" depending on its tones, so copy the melody you hear.

Igbo.title: Unit 3
Igbo.subtitle: Family
Igbo.tip: Respect for elders runs deep. Call an older man "Dede" or "Nna anyị" and an older woman "Daa" or "Nne anyị" instead of their first name.

Igbo.title: Unit 4
Igbo.subtitle: Numbers
Igbo.tip: Igbo numbers build on twenty (ọgụ): ọgụ is 20, ọgụ abụọ is 40. For everyday shopping, these ten numbers and "Ego ole?" get you far.

Igbo.title: Unit 5
Igbo.subtitle: Food and market
Igbo.tip: The Igbo week has four market days: Eke, Orie, Afọ and Nkwọ. Many towns name their big markets after the day they open, like Nkwọ Nnewi.

Igbo.title: Unit 6
Igbo.subtitle: At home
Igbo.tip: When you visit, the host offers kola nut (ọjị): "Onye wetara ọjị, wetara ndụ" - whoever brings kola brings life.

Igbo.title: Unit 7
Igbo.subtitle: Time and weather
Igbo.tip: Echi (tomorrow) and ụnyaahụ (yesterday) need no extra word: "Aga m abịa echi" means "I will come tomorrow".

Igbo.title: Unit 8
Igbo.subtitle: Questions and actions
Igbo.tip: Question words usually come first: "Gịnị ka ọ bụ?" (what is it?), "Onye bụ ya?" (who is it?), "Ebee ka ọ dị?" (where is it?).

Igbo.title: Unit 9
Igbo.subtitle: Feelings and body
Igbo.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Igbo.tip: The "m" at the end means "me" or "I": "Ike gwụrụ m" is literally "strength has finished me" - that is how Igbo says I am tired.

Igbo.title: Unit 10
Igbo.subtitle: Travel and help
Igbo.about: Find your way and ask for help
Igbo.tip: Aka nri is the right hand (the "eating hand") and aka ekpe the left. Always give and receive things with the right hand.

Swahili.title: Unit 1
Swahili.subtitle: Greetings
Swahili.tip: Swahili stress almost always falls on the second-to-last syllable: ha-BA-ri, a-SAN-te. Get this right and you sound natural straight away.

Swahili.title: Unit 2
Swahili.subtitle: Introductions
Swahili.tip: "Karibu" means welcome and also "you are welcome" after thanks. To a group say "Karibuni".

Swahili.title: Unit 3
Swahili.subtitle: Family
Swahili.tip: To greet an elder, say "Shikamoo". They answer "Marahaba". Using it shows real respect in Tanzania and on the coast.

Swahili.title: Unit 4
Swahili.subtitle: Numbers
Swahili.tip: Prices: "Bei gani?" (what price?). Shilingi is the money in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. Numbers above ten build on kumi: kumi na moja is 11.

Swahili.title: Unit 5
Swahili.subtitle: Food and market
Swahili.tip: Mchele is raw rice, wali is cooked rice. Swahili has different words for food at different stages - a sign of a cooking culture.

Swahili.title: Unit 6
Swahili.subtitle: At home
Swahili.tip: Swahili nouns come in classes that change the start of other words: kitabu kizuri (a good book) but vitabu vizuri (good books).

Swahili.title: Unit 7
Swahili.subtitle: Time and weather
Swahili.tip: Swahili time starts at sunrise: "saa moja asubuhi" (hour one in the morning) is 7 am. Add six hours to read it in clock time.

Swahili.title: Unit 8
Swahili.subtitle: Questions and actions
Swahili.tip: Verbs carry the person at the front: ni- (I), u- (you), a- (he/she). "Ninaenda" is ni + na (now) + enda (go): I am going.

Swahili.title: Unit 9
Swahili.subtitle: Feelings and body
Swahili.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Swahili.tip: The prefix ni- in "Nimechoka" means I and -me- means it has happened: I have become tired.

Swahili.title: Unit 10
Swahili.subtitle: Travel and help
Swahili.about: Find your way and ask for help
Swahili.tip: "Pole pole" means slowly, gently. "Safari njema" (good journey) is what you say to anyone who is travelling.

Zulu.title: Unit 1
Zulu.subtitle: Greetings
Zulu.tip: "Sawubona" literally means "we see you" and works all day; answer "Yebo, sawubona". To a group say "Sanibonani". Time-of-day greetings are used less often.

Zulu.title: Unit 2
Zulu.subtitle: Introductions
Zulu.tip: Zulu has three clicks: c (tongue off the teeth, like "tsk"), q (a pop from the roof of the mouth) and x (from the side of the mouth). Practise them slowly.

Zulu.title: Unit 3
Zulu.subtitle: Family
Zulu.tip: The prefix u-/um- marks a person: umama, ubaba, umngane. Grandmother is "ugogo" and people of that age are greeted with real respect.

Zulu.title: Unit 4
Zulu.subtitle: Numbers
Zulu.tip: Numbers 6 to 9 are long because they are descriptions: isishiyagalombili means "leave out two" (ten minus two = eight).

Zulu.title: Unit 5
Zulu.subtitle: Food and market
Zulu.tip: "Malini?" (how much?) comes from imali (money). Street markets and taxi ranks are where you hear the most Zulu.

Zulu.title: Unit 6
Zulu.subtitle: At home
Zulu.tip: "Ngena" (come in) and "Hlala phansi" (sit down) are what a host says. You greet the people of the house before anything else.

Zulu.title: Unit 7
Zulu.subtitle: Time and weather
Zulu.tip: "Kusasa" (tomorrow) also means early morning. "Izolo" is yesterday. Zulu verbs change their ending for past: ngilambile (I am hungry - it has happened).

Zulu.title: Unit 8
Zulu.subtitle: Questions and actions
Zulu.tip: Questions use a question word at the end or the start: "Uyaphi?" (where are you going?) or "Kuphi?" (where?).

Zulu.title: Unit 9
Zulu.subtitle: Feelings and body
Zulu.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Zulu.tip: Most verbs start with ngi- for "I": ngiyagula (I am sick), ngikhathele (I am tired), ngiyakuthanda (I love you).

Zulu.title: Unit 10
Zulu.subtitle: Travel and help
Zulu.about: Find your way and ask for help
Zulu.tip: Goodbye depends on who leaves: the one going says "Sala kahle" (stay well), the one staying says "Hamba kahle" (go well).

Twi.title: Unit 1
Twi.subtitle: Greetings
Twi.tip: Maakye, maaha and maadwo are morning, afternoon and evening greetings. The reply is "Yaa nua" (to a peer), "Yaa agya" (to a man) or "Yaa ɛna" (to a woman).

Twi.title: Unit 2
Twi.subtitle: Introductions
Twi.tip: Twi is tonal and has two extra vowels: ɛ (as in "bed") and ɔ (as in "law"). Wo (you) and wɔ (they are at) are different words.

Twi.title: Unit 3
Twi.subtitle: Family
Twi.tip: Akan people have day names: a boy born on Saturday is Kwame and a girl born on Sunday is Akosua. Ask someone their day name!

Twi.title: Unit 4
Twi.subtitle: Numbers
Twi.tip: Ghana uses the cedi. "Ɛyɛ sɛn?" (how much is it?) works in any market. Twi numbers above ten add to edu: edu baako is eleven.

Twi.title: Unit 5
Twi.subtitle: Food and market
Twi.tip: In the market, a gentle "te so" (reduce it) usually gets a better price. Sellers may add a small extra called "ntosoɔ".

Twi.title: Unit 6
Twi.subtitle: At home
Twi.tip: Before entering a compound, call out "Agoo!" and wait for "Amee!" - it is the polite way to announce yourself.

Twi.title: Unit 7
Twi.subtitle: Time and weather
Twi.tip: Ɛnnɛ (today), ɔkyena (tomorrow), ɛnnora (yesterday). Time of day in Twi starts with "abɔ" - the clock "has struck".

Twi.title: Unit 8
Twi.subtitle: Questions and actions
Twi.tip: Twi question words: ɛdeɛn (what), hwan (who), ɛhe (where), adɛn (why), daben (when). "Wo" means you and "me" means I or my.

Twi.title: Unit 9
Twi.subtitle: Feelings and body
Twi.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Twi.tip: Twi uses the left hand only for the toilet - always greet, give and eat with the right hand.

Twi.title: Unit 10
Twi.subtitle: Travel and help
Twi.about: Find your way and ask for help
Twi.tip: "Nantew yie" (walk well) is goodbye; "Akwantu pa" wishes a good journey.

Amharic.title: Unit 1
Amharic.subtitle: Greetings
Amharic.tip: Amharic greetings change with the time of day: እንደምን አደሩ (how did you pass the night) in the morning, ዋሉ (the day) in the afternoon, አመሹ (the evening) at night. These forms are the polite ones for elders.

Amharic.title: Unit 2
Amharic.subtitle: Introductions
Amharic.tip: Amharic changes words for who you talk to: ነህ (to a man), ነሽ (to a woman), ኖት (polite). "እንዴት ነህ?" becomes "እንዴት ነሽ?" for a woman.

Amharic.title: Unit 3
Amharic.subtitle: Family
Amharic.tip: Amharic is written in Ge'ez (ፊደል): each letter is a syllable, like ቤ (be) or ተ (te). There are over 200 letters made from 33 base shapes.

Amharic.title: Unit 4
Amharic.subtitle: Numbers
Amharic.tip: Prices are in birr. "ስንት ነው?" (how much is it?) is the key market phrase. Ethiopia also has its own calendar of 13 months and is about seven to eight years behind the Western one.

Amharic.title: Unit 5
Amharic.subtitle: Food and market
Amharic.tip: Meals are shared from one big plate of injera. Feeding someone a bite by hand, called gursha, is a sign of love and respect.

Amharic.title: Unit 6
Amharic.subtitle: At home
Amharic.tip: Coffee comes from Ethiopia. A visitor is often invited to a coffee ceremony with three rounds: abol, tona and baraka.

Amharic.title: Unit 7
Amharic.subtitle: Time and weather
Amharic.tip: Ethiopian time counts from sunrise: 1 o'clock (አንድ ሰዓት) is 7 am. Always check which clock someone means!

Amharic.title: Unit 8
Amharic.subtitle: Questions and actions
Amharic.tip: Amharic verbs go at the end of the sentence: "ገበያው የት ነው?" is literally "the market where is?".

Amharic.title: Unit 9
Amharic.subtitle: Feelings and body
Amharic.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Amharic.tip: Feelings often use a "to me" ending -ኛል: ርቦኛል (hunger has struck me = I am hungry), ደክሞኛል (I am tired).

Amharic.title: Unit 10
Amharic.subtitle: Travel and help
Amharic.about: Find your way and ask for help
Amharic.tip: "መልካም ጉዞ" (good journey) is said to travellers. ግራ is left and ቀኝ is right.

Xhosa.title: Unit 1
Xhosa.subtitle: Greetings
Xhosa.tip: "Molo" is hello to one person, "Molweni" to a group, and it works at any time of day. The answer is "Ewe, molo".

Xhosa.title: Unit 2
Xhosa.subtitle: Introductions
Xhosa.tip: Xhosa has many clicks: c (teeth, like "tsk"), q (roof of the mouth, a pop) and x (side of the mouth, like calling a horse). The name isiXhosa itself starts with the x click.

Xhosa.title: Unit 3
Xhosa.subtitle: Family
Xhosa.tip: Family words carry respect: "utata" (father) is also how you address any older man, and "umama" any older woman.

Xhosa.title: Unit 4
Xhosa.subtitle: Numbers
Xhosa.tip: Numbers agree with what you count: "abantu ababini" (two people) but "izinja ezimbini" (two dogs). When just counting, people often switch to English.

Xhosa.title: Unit 5
Xhosa.subtitle: Food and market
Xhosa.tip: "Yimalini?" means "how much is it?". Imali is money; the R in prices is the South African rand.

Xhosa.title: Unit 6
Xhosa.subtitle: At home
Xhosa.tip: Visitors are welcomed with "Wamkelekile". Wait to be offered a seat, and greet everyone in the room.

Xhosa.title: Unit 7
Xhosa.subtitle: Time and weather
Xhosa.tip: "Kusasa" means morning and "ngomso" means tomorrow. Xhosa time words often start with ngo-, meaning "at": ngokuhlwa (in the evening).

Xhosa.title: Unit 8
Xhosa.subtitle: Questions and actions
Xhosa.tip: "Kutheni?" (why?) and "Ngubani?" (who?) start the sentence; "Phi?" (where?) is usually added to the end of a verb: "Uyaphi?" (where are you going?).

Xhosa.title: Unit 9
Xhosa.subtitle: Feelings and body
Xhosa.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Xhosa.tip: Verbs for "I" start with ndi-: ndiyagula (I am sick), ndidiniwe (I am tired), ndiyakuthanda (I love you).

Xhosa.title: Unit 10
Xhosa.subtitle: Travel and help
Xhosa.about: Find your way and ask for help
Xhosa.tip: Say "Hamba kakuhle" (go well) to someone leaving and "Sala kakuhle" (stay well) to someone staying.

Shona.title: Unit 1
Shona.subtitle: Greetings
Shona.tip: Shona greets by the time of day: mangwanani (morning), masikati (afternoon), manheru (evening). Clap your cupped hands softly when greeting an elder.

Shona.title: Unit 2
Shona.subtitle: Introductions
Shona.tip: Use the plural forms (makadii, pindai, garai) for one person to show respect. Singular forms are for friends and children.

Shona.title: Unit 3
Shona.subtitle: Family
Shona.tip: "Amai" (mother) and "baba" (father) are also respectful ways to address any adult woman or man. Your father's sister is "vatete", an important adviser in the family.

Shona.title: Unit 4
Shona.subtitle: Numbers
Shona.tip: Counting objects changes the numbers to agree with them: "vanhu vaviri" (two people). The forms here are the plain counting numbers.

Shona.title: Unit 5
Shona.subtitle: Food and market
Shona.tip: In the market, "Imarii?" means "how much is it?". Sellers often round prices; a friendly greeting first makes bargaining easier.

Shona.title: Unit 6
Shona.subtitle: At home
Shona.tip: When visiting, wait outside and call "Gogogoi!" (knock knock). The host answers "Pindai" (come in).

Shona.title: Unit 7
Shona.subtitle: Time and weather
Shona.tip: Mangwana is tomorrow and nezuro is yesterday. Notice that mangwana (tomorrow) is close to mangwanani (morning).

Shona.title: Unit 8
Shona.subtitle: Questions and actions
Shona.tip: Questions usually put the question word at the end: "Musika uri kupi?" (the market is where?).

Shona.title: Unit 9
Shona.subtitle: Feelings and body
Shona.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Shona.tip: Many verbs start with "ndi-" for I: ndinofara (I am happy), ndinorwara (I am sick), ndinokuda (I love you).

Shona.title: Unit 10
Shona.subtitle: Travel and help
Shona.about: Find your way and ask for help
Shona.tip: The one leaving says "Chisarai zvakanaka" (stay well); the one staying says "Fambai zvakanaka" (go well).

Wolof.title: Unit 1
Wolof.subtitle: Greetings
Wolof.tip: Wolof greetings are a ritual: "Salaam aleekum" is answered "Maleekum salaam", then you ask about health, family and work. Skipping them feels rude.

Wolof.title: Unit 2
Wolof.subtitle: Introductions
Wolof.tip: Wolof puts the name before "laa": "Moussa laa tudd" is "Moussa is what I am called". This focus word order is very common in Wolof.

Wolof.title: Unit 3
Wolof.subtitle: Family
Wolof.tip: Senegal is known for teranga - hospitality. Guests are offered food and the famous three rounds of attaya tea.

Wolof.title: Unit 4
Wolof.subtitle: Numbers
Wolof.tip: Wolof counts in fives: juróom is five, so six is juróom benn (five-one) and seven juróom ñaar (five-two).

Wolof.title: Unit 5
Wolof.subtitle: Food and market
Wolof.tip: Prices are in CFA francs and often said in "dërëm" (units of five francs) by older sellers - a classic surprise for newcomers.

Wolof.title: Unit 6
Wolof.subtitle: At home
Wolof.tip: The family meal is eaten from one big bowl (bol). Eat from the part in front of you with your right hand.

Wolof.title: Unit 7
Wolof.subtitle: Time and weather
Wolof.tip: Many verbs start with "dafa" (it is) to describe a state: dafa tàng (it is hot), dafa sedd (it is cold).

Wolof.title: Unit 8
Wolof.subtitle: Questions and actions
Wolof.tip: Question words come first: "Fan la marse bi nekk?" is "Where is the market?" - literally "where is the market located?".

Wolof.title: Unit 9
Wolof.subtitle: Feelings and body
Wolof.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Wolof.tip: "Dama" means "I am / I do": dama sonn (I am tired), dama xiif (I am hungry), dama la bëgg (I love you).

Wolof.title: Unit 10
Wolof.subtitle: Travel and help
Wolof.about: Find your way and ask for help
Wolof.tip: Senegal's wrestling (laamb) is the national sport, and "Jàmm" (peace) is the most important word in greetings.

Somali.title: Unit 1
Somali.subtitle: Greetings
Somali.tip: Somali greetings use "wanaagsan" (good): subax wanaagsan (good morning), galab (afternoon), fiid (evening). "Nabad" (peace) is the key word of many greetings.

Somali.title: Unit 2
Somali.subtitle: Introductions
Somali.tip: Somali spelling has its own letters: c is a deep throat sound (as in Cabdi = Abdi), x is a breathy h, q is a k from the back of the throat and dh is a strong d.

Somali.title: Unit 3
Somali.subtitle: Family
Somali.tip: Hooyo (mother) and aabe (father) are also how you call any older woman or man. Family lineage (clan) is very important to Somalis.

Somali.title: Unit 4
Somali.subtitle: Numbers
Somali.tip: Somali numbers above ten add "iyo" (and): toban iyo kow is eleven. "Waa imisa?" means "how much is it?".

Somali.title: Unit 5
Somali.subtitle: Food and market
Somali.tip: Somalis drink spiced tea (shaah) and eat rice or pasta (baasto, from Italian) with banana on the side!

Somali.title: Unit 6
Somali.subtitle: At home
Somali.tip: Somali has a "focus" word like "baa" or "ayaa" that marks the important part: "Biyo ayaan rabaa" = it is WATER I want.

Somali.title: Unit 7
Somali.subtitle: Time and weather
Somali.tip: Maanta (today), berri (tomorrow) and shalay (yesterday) usually go at the start of the sentence.

Somali.title: Unit 8
Somali.subtitle: Questions and actions
Somali.tip: Somali verbs come at the end of the sentence, and question words often take the focus word: "Xagee baad ka timid?"

Somali.title: Unit 9
Somali.subtitle: Feelings and body
Somali.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Somali.tip: Feelings end in -ahay for "I am": waan faraxsanahay (I am happy), waan daalanahay (I am tired).

Somali.title: Unit 10
Somali.subtitle: Travel and help
Somali.about: Find your way and ask for help
Somali.tip: Somalia has the longest coastline in mainland Africa. "Safar wanaagsan" wishes someone a good journey.

Oromo.title: Unit 1
Oromo.subtitle: Greetings
Oromo.tip: Oromo greetings ask how you spent the time: "Akkam bultan?" (how did you spend the night) in the morning and "Akkam ooltan?" (the day) later. "Nagaa" means peace.

Oromo.title: Unit 2
Oromo.subtitle: Introductions
Oromo.tip: Oromo is written in the Latin alphabet called Qubee. Double letters are held longer: "lama" (two) and "laamaa" sound different. C is an explosive ch', x an explosive t'.

Oromo.title: Unit 3
Oromo.subtitle: Family
Oromo.tip: Elders are greatly respected; the traditional Gadaa system organises society by age groups that take turns leading.

Oromo.title: Unit 4
Oromo.subtitle: Numbers
Oromo.tip: Numbers above ten add "-tama" for tens: digdama is twenty. "Meeqa?" means "how much / how many?".

Oromo.title: Unit 5
Oromo.subtitle: Food and market
Oromo.tip: Coffee (buna) comes from the Oromo region of Ethiopia, and buna qalaa (coffee cooked in butter) is a traditional welcome.

Oromo.title: Unit 6
Oromo.subtitle: At home
Oromo.tip: "Mana" means house; many places are "mana + something": mana barumsaa (house of learning = school), mana fincaanii (toilet).

Oromo.title: Unit 7
Oromo.subtitle: Time and weather
Oromo.tip: Time words come first: "Boru dhufa" (I will come tomorrow), "Har'a" (today), "Kaleessa" (yesterday).

Oromo.title: Unit 8
Oromo.subtitle: Questions and actions
Oromo.tip: Oromo verbs come at the end and many sentences end with "dha" (is): "Bishaan qorraa dha" (the water is cold).

Oromo.title: Unit 9
Oromo.subtitle: Feelings and body
Oromo.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Oromo.tip: The ending -eera shows something that has happened to you: gammadeera (I have become happy), dadhabeera (I am tired).

Oromo.title: Unit 10
Oromo.subtitle: Travel and help
Oromo.about: Find your way and ask for help
Oromo.tip: "Karaa nagaa" means "road of peace" - a safe journey. Mirga is right and bitaa is left.

Lingala.title: Unit 1
Lingala.subtitle: Greetings
Lingala.tip: "Mbote" is hello at any time of day; add "ya ntɔ́ngó" for the morning. To a group say "Mbote na bino".

Lingala.title: Unit 2
Lingala.subtitle: Introductions
Lingala.tip: Lingala is the language of Congolese rumba and soukous. Lingala has seven vowels: ɛ (as in "bed") and ɔ (as in "law") are different from e and o.

Lingala.title: Unit 3
Lingala.subtitle: Family
Lingala.tip: Any older woman can be called "Mama" and any older man "Tata" as a sign of respect - even strangers in the street.

Lingala.title: Unit 4
Lingala.subtitle: Numbers
Lingala.tip: Prices are asked with "Ntalo bóni?" (what price?). In Kinshasa people often mix Lingala and French numbers when shopping.

Lingala.title: Unit 5
Lingala.subtitle: Food and market
Lingala.tip: Fufu, pondu (cassava leaves) and grilled fish (mbisi) are favourite dishes. "Elengi" means sweet or delicious - and also enjoyable.

Lingala.title: Unit 6
Lingala.subtitle: At home
Lingala.tip: "Kɔtá" (come in) and "Fánda" (sit down) are what you hear when visiting. Greet everyone first.

Lingala.title: Unit 7
Lingala.subtitle: Time and weather
Lingala.tip: Lóbí means both tomorrow AND yesterday! Context or the verb tense tells you which: "lóbí eleki" (the lóbí that passed) is clearly yesterday.

Lingala.title: Unit 8
Lingala.subtitle: Questions and actions
Lingala.tip: Questions often keep normal word order with the question word at the end: "Zándo ezali wapi?" (the market is where?).

Lingala.title: Unit 9
Lingala.subtitle: Feelings and body
Lingala.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Lingala.tip: Na- is "I": nalingi (I want / I love), nalɛmbi (I am tired), nasepeli (I am happy).

Lingala.title: Unit 10
Lingala.subtitle: Travel and help
Lingala.about: Find your way and ask for help
Lingala.tip: Left is "the woman's hand" (lobɔ́kɔ ya mwási) and right is "the man's hand" (lobɔ́kɔ ya mobáli).

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 1
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: Greetings
Kinyarwanda.tip: "Mwaramutse" is good morning (until about noon) and "Mwiriwe" is used for the afternoon. The mu-/mw- forms are polite or plural; to one friend say "Waramutse".

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 2
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: Introductions
Kinyarwanda.tip: Kinyarwanda is tonal and spoken by almost everyone in Rwanda. "Murakaza neza" (welcome) is one of the first phrases visitors hear.

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 3
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: Family
Kinyarwanda.tip: Umuryango means family and also community. Respect for parents and elders is shown by using plural "mu-" forms when speaking to them.

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 4
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: Numbers
Kinyarwanda.tip: Rwanda uses the Rwandan franc: "Ni angahe?" asks the price. Numbers agree with what you count: "abantu babiri" (two people).

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 5
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: Food and market
Kinyarwanda.tip: Brochettes (grilled skewers), isombe (cassava leaves) and plantain (ibitoki) are everyday foods.

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 6
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: At home
Kinyarwanda.tip: Umuganda is the national community work day on the last Saturday of the month, when neighbours clean and build together.

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 7
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: Time and weather
Kinyarwanda.tip: Ejo means both tomorrow and yesterday; the verb tense shows which. "Ejo hashize" (ejo that has passed) makes yesterday clear.

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 8
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: Questions and actions
Kinyarwanda.tip: Question words come at the end: "Isoko riri he?" (the market is where?), "Uriya ni nde?" (that one is who?).

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 9
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: Feelings and body
Kinyarwanda.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Kinyarwanda.tip: The prefix nda- usually means "I am": ndashonje (I am hungry), ndananiwe (I am tired), ndarwaye (I am sick).

Kinyarwanda.title: Unit 10
Kinyarwanda.subtitle: Travel and help
Kinyarwanda.about: Find your way and ask for help
Kinyarwanda.tip: Rwanda is called "the land of a thousand hills" (igihugu cy'imisozi igihumbi), so roads wind a lot - "Urugendo ruhire" (safe journey)!

Luganda.title: Unit 1
Luganda.subtitle: Greetings
Luganda.tip: Baganda greet a lot: "Gyebale ko" (well done, thank you for your work) is said to anyone working. Women and girls traditionally kneel to greet elders.

Luganda.title: Unit 2
Luganda.subtitle: Introductions
Luganda.tip: Double consonants are held longer and change meaning: "ssente" (money) starts with a long s. Luganda is tonal, but the doubled sounds matter most for beginners.

Luganda.title: Unit 3
Luganda.subtitle: Family
Luganda.tip: Children often carry clan names: Nakato is the name for an elder twin girl, and Mukasa is linked to the god of Lake Victoria in Buganda tradition.

Luganda.title: Unit 4
Luganda.subtitle: Numbers
Luganda.tip: Uganda uses the shilling: "Ssente mmeka?" (how much money?). Prices are often in thousands - "lukumi" is a thousand.

Luganda.title: Unit 5
Luganda.subtitle: Food and market
Luganda.tip: Matooke (steamed green banana) is the heart of a Ganda meal, served with groundnut sauce or meat.

Luganda.title: Unit 6
Luganda.subtitle: At home
Luganda.tip: Visitors are always offered something - at least water or tea. "Tukusanyukidde" means "we are happy to have you".

Luganda.title: Unit 7
Luganda.subtitle: Time and weather
Luganda.tip: Leero (today), enkya (tomorrow) and jjo (yesterday) usually come at the end of the sentence: "Nja kujja enkya" (I will come tomorrow).

Luganda.title: Unit 8
Luganda.subtitle: Questions and actions
Luganda.tip: "Ludda wa?" means "which side?" and is used for asking where things are: "Akatale kali ludda wa?".

Luganda.title: Unit 9
Luganda.subtitle: Feelings and body
Luganda.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Luganda.tip: Many "I" verbs start with n-: nsanyuse (I am happy), nkooye (I am tired), nkwagala (I love you).

Luganda.title: Unit 10
Luganda.subtitle: Travel and help
Luganda.about: Find your way and ask for help
Luganda.tip: Boda-bodas (motorbike taxis) are everywhere in Kampala. Tell the rider "Yimirira wano" (stop here) when you arrive.

Sesotho.title: Unit 1
Sesotho.subtitle: Greetings
Sesotho.tip: "Lumela" is hello to one person and "Lumelang" to a group. The national motto of Lesotho is "Khotso, Pula, Nala" - peace, rain, prosperity - and "Khotso" is also used as a greeting.

Sesotho.title: Unit 2
Sesotho.subtitle: Introductions
Sesotho.tip: Sesotho spelling in Lesotho writes "li" and "lu" but they sound like "di" and "du": "lijo" (food) is said "dijo".

Sesotho.title: Unit 3
Sesotho.subtitle: Family
Sesotho.tip: Call older men "Ntate" and older women "'Mè" - it is respectful even to strangers. Sesotho kings and chiefs are greatly honoured.

Sesotho.title: Unit 4
Sesotho.subtitle: Numbers
Sesotho.tip: Lesotho uses the loti (plural maloti), equal to the South African rand. "Ke bokae?" asks how much.

Sesotho.title: Unit 5
Sesotho.subtitle: Food and market
Sesotho.tip: Papa (stiff maize porridge) is the staple, eaten with moroho (greens) and meat.

Sesotho.title: Unit 6
Sesotho.subtitle: At home
Sesotho.tip: Lesotho is the "Kingdom in the Sky": the whole country is above 1,000 metres, so homes are built for the cold.

Sesotho.title: Unit 7
Sesotho.subtitle: Time and weather
Sesotho.tip: Ho a chesa (it is hot) and ho a bata (it is cold) - in the highlands snow falls in winter, which surprises many visitors.

Sesotho.title: Unit 8
Sesotho.subtitle: Questions and actions
Sesotho.tip: Question words usually go at the end: "'Maraka o kae?" (the market is where?), "U tsoa kae?" (you come from where?).

Sesotho.title: Unit 9
Sesotho.subtitle: Feelings and body
Sesotho.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Sesotho.tip: Ke means "I": ke thabile (I am happy), ke khathetse (I am tired), ke a kula (I am sick).

Sesotho.title: Unit 10
Sesotho.subtitle: Travel and help
Sesotho.about: Find your way and ask for help
Sesotho.tip: The Basotho blanket and the mokorotlo (cone-shaped hat) are national symbols you will see on any journey.

Afrikaans.title: Unit 1
Afrikaans.subtitle: Greetings
Afrikaans.tip: Afrikaans grew out of Dutch at the Cape, mixed with Malay, Portuguese, Khoekhoe and Bantu languages. "Goeiemôre" (good morning) is "goede morgen" in Dutch.

Afrikaans.title: Unit 2
Afrikaans.subtitle: Introductions
Afrikaans.tip: The g in Afrikaans is a rough throat sound like ch in Scottish "loch": "goed" is said "khoot". The w sounds like v.

Afrikaans.title: Unit 3
Afrikaans.subtitle: Family
Afrikaans.tip: Older people are often called "Oom" (uncle) and "Tannie" (aunt) even if they are not family - it is respectful and warm.

Afrikaans.title: Unit 4
Afrikaans.subtitle: Numbers
Afrikaans.tip: Afrikaans says numbers above 20 backwards like Dutch: 21 is "een-en-twintig" (one-and-twenty). "Hoeveel kos dit?" asks the price.

Afrikaans.title: Unit 5
Afrikaans.subtitle: Food and market
Afrikaans.tip: A braai (barbecue) is the heart of social life, with boerewors (farmer's sausage) and pap (maize porridge).

Afrikaans.title: Unit 6
Afrikaans.subtitle: At home
Afrikaans.tip: Afrikaans has very little grammar change: verbs are the same for I, you and they - "ek is, jy is, hulle is".

Afrikaans.title: Unit 7
Afrikaans.subtitle: Time and weather
Afrikaans.tip: Time words move the verb: "Môre gaan ek werk" (tomorrow go I work) - the verb is always in second place.

Afrikaans.title: Unit 8
Afrikaans.subtitle: Questions and actions
Afrikaans.tip: Afrikaans often uses a double negative: "Ek het dit nie gesien nie" (I did not see it) - a second "nie" closes the sentence.

Afrikaans.title: Unit 9
Afrikaans.subtitle: Feelings and body
Afrikaans.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Afrikaans.tip: "Lekker" is the most famous Afrikaans word - nice, tasty, fun, great - and even English-speaking South Africans use it.

Afrikaans.title: Unit 10
Afrikaans.subtitle: Travel and help
Afrikaans.about: Find your way and ask for help
Afrikaans.tip: A "robot" in South Africa is a traffic light: "Draai links by die robot" means turn left at the traffic light.

Setswana.title: Unit 1
Setswana.subtitle: Greetings
Setswana.tip: "Dumela rra" (to a man) and "Dumela mma" (to a woman) are the polite greetings. In the morning ask "O tsogile jang?" (how did you wake up?) and later "O tlhotse jang?" (how did you spend the day?).

Setswana.title: Unit 2
Setswana.subtitle: Introductions
Setswana.tip: In Setswana the letter g is a soft throat sound like h in "Gaborone" (ha-bo-RO-neh). Kg is a stronger, rasping k.

Setswana.title: Unit 3
Setswana.subtitle: Family
Setswana.tip: Rre (sir, father) and mmê (madam, mother) are used for any adult. Children are taught to greet every elder they meet.

Setswana.title: Unit 4
Setswana.subtitle: Numbers
Setswana.tip: Botswana uses the pula - the word for rain, the most precious thing in a dry country. "Ke bokae?" asks the price.

Setswana.title: Unit 5
Setswana.subtitle: Food and market
Setswana.tip: Seswaa (pounded beef) with bogobe (porridge) is the national dish, served at weddings and celebrations.

Setswana.title: Unit 6
Setswana.subtitle: At home
Setswana.tip: When visiting, wait at the gate (kgoro) and call out "Ko ko!" until someone welcomes you in.

Setswana.title: Unit 7
Setswana.subtitle: Time and weather
Setswana.tip: Kamoso is tomorrow and maabane yesterday. Rain (pula) is shouted at the end of speeches as a blessing: "Pula!"

Setswana.title: Unit 8
Setswana.subtitle: Questions and actions
Setswana.tip: Questions are often marked just by "a" at the start: "A o bua Sekgoa?" (do you speak English?).

Setswana.title: Unit 9
Setswana.subtitle: Feelings and body
Setswana.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Setswana.tip: Ke means I: ke itumetse (I am happy), ke lapile (I am tired), ke a lwala (I am sick).

Setswana.title: Unit 10
Setswana.subtitle: Travel and help
Setswana.about: Find your way and ask for help
Setswana.tip: "Tsamaya sentle" (go well) is said to someone leaving; they answer "Sala sentle" (stay well).

Chichewa.title: Unit 1
Chichewa.subtitle: Greetings
Chichewa.tip: Malawi is called "the warm heart of Africa". Greetings ask how you woke (mwadzuka bwanji?) or spent the day (mwaswera bwanji?). Answer "Ndadzuka bwino" or "Ndaswera bwino".

Chichewa.title: Unit 2
Chichewa.subtitle: Introductions
Chichewa.tip: Use the polite -ni forms (lowani, khalani, pepani) for adults and strangers; drop -ni only with close friends and children.

Chichewa.title: Unit 3
Chichewa.subtitle: Family
Chichewa.tip: Agogo means grandparent; add aakazi (female) or aamuna (male). Grandparents are honoured and often help raise the children.

Chichewa.title: Unit 4
Chichewa.subtitle: Numbers
Chichewa.tip: Six to nine are built on five: "zisanu ndi chimodzi" is five and one. Malawi uses the kwacha, which means "dawn".

Chichewa.title: Unit 5
Chichewa.subtitle: Food and market
Chichewa.tip: Nsima (stiff maize porridge) is the staple. Chambo, a fish from Lake Malawi, is the national favourite.

Chichewa.title: Unit 6
Chichewa.subtitle: At home
Chichewa.tip: Before entering, say "Odi!" (may I come in?) and wait for "Lowani!" (come in).

Chichewa.title: Unit 7
Chichewa.subtitle: Time and weather
Chichewa.tip: Mawa is tomorrow and m'mawa (with the apostrophe) is morning; dzulo is yesterday.

Chichewa.title: Unit 8
Chichewa.subtitle: Questions and actions
Chichewa.tip: Questions often end with the question word: "Msika uli kuti?" (the market is where?), "Uyo ndani?" (that is who?).

Chichewa.title: Unit 9
Chichewa.subtitle: Feelings and body
Chichewa.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Chichewa.tip: Nd- means I: ndatopa (I am tired), ndikudwala (I am sick), ndimakukonda (I love you).

Chichewa.title: Unit 10
Chichewa.subtitle: Travel and help
Chichewa.about: Find your way and ask for help
Chichewa.tip: "Ulendo wabwino" (good journey) - and Lake Malawi, the third largest lake in Africa, is a journey worth taking.

Malagasy.title: Unit 1
Malagasy.subtitle: Greetings
Malagasy.tip: Malagasy came from Borneo across the Indian Ocean about 1,500 years ago - it is related to languages of Indonesia, not mainland Africa. Add "tompoko" (sir / madam) to be polite.

Malagasy.title: Unit 2
Malagasy.subtitle: Introductions
Malagasy.tip: Malagasy swallows the end of most words: a final -a, -y or -o is barely said, so "Misaotra" sounds like "mee-SOWTCH". Tr sounds like "tch".

Malagasy.title: Unit 3
Malagasy.subtitle: Family
Malagasy.tip: Older relatives are honoured even after death: the famadihana ceremony re-wraps ancestors' remains in new cloth with music and dancing.

Malagasy.title: Unit 4
Malagasy.subtitle: Numbers
Malagasy.tip: Madagascar uses the ariary. "Ohatrinona?" (how much?) is the market question; prices were once given in "francs" worth a fifth of an ariary.

Malagasy.title: Unit 5
Malagasy.subtitle: Food and market
Malagasy.tip: Rice (vary) is eaten three times a day - Malagasy people eat more rice per person than almost anyone in the world.

Malagasy.title: Unit 6
Malagasy.subtitle: At home
Malagasy.tip: Malagasy sentences put the verb first and the person last: "Mila rano aho" is literally "need water I".

Malagasy.title: Unit 7
Malagasy.subtitle: Time and weather
Malagasy.tip: Rahampitso is tomorrow and omaly yesterday. Androany (today) comes from andro, the word for day.

Malagasy.title: Unit 8
Malagasy.subtitle: Questions and actions
Malagasy.tip: Many questions start with a question word and "no": "Iza no anaranao?" (who is your name? = what is your name?).

Malagasy.title: Unit 9
Malagasy.subtitle: Feelings and body
Malagasy.about: How you feel and where it hurts
Malagasy.tip: "Aho" (I) comes at the end: faly aho (I am happy), reraka aho (I am tired), marary aho (I am sick).

Malagasy.title: Unit 10
Malagasy.subtitle: Travel and help
Malagasy.about: Find your way and ask for help
Malagasy.tip: "Mora mora" (slowly, slowly) is the Malagasy way of life - and the answer to most travel questions!
